article_title: Fluency Formula (Beginning Reading)
citation: Fluency Formula™ WWC Intervention Report. (2007). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://teacher.scholastic.com/products/fluencyformula/pdfs/FF_EffectivessReport.pdf
title: Weekly instructional cycle combining whole-class fluency instruction with ability-differentiated small-group practice
description: The program organizes instruction as a five-day weekly cycle: "The first two days of each instructional week are devoted to direct instruction and guided practice activities for the whole class" focused on fluent reading, prosody, and oral comprehension. On the next two days, students reading at or above grade level practice fluency independently while below-grade-level students receive small-group instruction emphasizing phonics and word attack skills; the fifth day is used for assessment-based identification of struggling students and goal setting.
requirements: Use of the Fluency Formula™ Assessment System on the fifth day to identify struggling students and set instructional goals
Teachers model fluent reading and lead repeated, partner, and choral reading practice
constraints: In the evaluated study, low initial-ability students received four days a week of instruction while high initial-ability students received only two days of whole-class instruction
target_learners: first- through sixth-grade students reading below, at, or above grade level
target_learning_goals: reading fluency
prosody
phonics and word attack skills
oral comprehension
examples: Students classified as low initial ability received two days of whole-class plus two days of small-group Fluency Formula™ instruction weekly
key_sources: Fluency Formula™ WWC Intervention Report. (2007). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://teacher.scholastic.com/products/fluencyformula/pdfs/FF_EffectivessReport.pdf

article_title: Rolling Back Zero Tolerance: The Effect of Discipline Policy Reform on Suspension Usage and Student Outcomes
citation: Johanna Lacoe, Matthew P. Steinberg. (2018). Rolling Back Zero Tolerance: The Effect of Discipline Policy Reform on Suspension Usage and Student Outcomes. Peabody Journal of Education, vol. 93, issue 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/rolling-back-zero-tolerance-the-effect-of-discipline-policy-reform-on-suspension-usage-and-student-outcomes
title: Policymakers should weigh suspension-usage and student-outcome consequences when designing district-level discipline reforms
description: The article's stated purpose is that its findings "should inform policymakers and practitioners on the implications of district-level reforms for suspension usage and the potential consequences for student outcomes." Districts revising zero-tolerance policies toward "more tempered disciplinary responses" should anticipate that limiting suspensions for nonviolent misconduct may not reduce total suspensions and may coincide with increased serious incidents, truancy, and achievement decline.
requirements: District-level policy reform context with administrative data on suspensions, incidents, truancy, and achievement to monitor outcomes
constraints: Findings are from one district (Philadelphia) reform in 2012-2013; the article reports associations following the reform via difference-in-differences, not tested mechanisms
target_learners: K-12 students in districts revising zero-tolerance discipline policies
target_learning_goals: Student attendance and academic achievement in math and English language arts
examples: Philadelphia's 2012-2013 reform limited suspensions for nonviolent student misconduct and granted principals greater discretion over more serious misconduct.

article_title: The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions (Journal Article)
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2010). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 35, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use pretest-posttest designs in education RCTs to improve precision of estimated treatment effects, but weigh the bias risk of late pretests
description: Education RCTs often use pretest-posttest designs because including pretests improves the precision of estimated treatment effects. However, when pretests are collected after random assignment, analysts should not automatically include them: the decision "involves a variance-bias trade-off" that should be evaluated using a loss function approach before late pretest data are used in impact estimation.
requirements: RCT designs where pretest data collection timing relative to random assignment is known
constraints: Bias risk applies specifically when pretest data are collected after random assignment for logistical reasons
target_learners: Education researchers, evaluators, and analysts conducting randomized control trials
target_learning_goals: Designing RCT analyses that balance precision against bias in treatment effect estimates
examples: The article analyzes the trade-off theoretically and empirically for several commonly used impact estimators in education RCTs.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2010). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 35, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/journal-article-the-late-pretest-problem-in-randomized-control-trials-of-education-interventions

article_title: Identifying Students At Risk Using Prior Performance Versus a Machine Learning Algorithm
citation: Lindsay Cattell, Julie Bruch. (2021). Identifying Students At Risk Using Prior Performance Versus a Machine Learning Algorithm. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Choose between prior-performance flags and algorithmic risk scores by weighing accuracy needs against cost, ease of setup, and the value of fine-grained risk information
description: The report presents the choice of early warning approach as a tradeoff rather than a single best option. It notes the prior performance system "is just as accurate as the algorithm for some purposes and is cheaper and easier to set up, but it does not provide fine-grained information." Districts needing to distinguish degrees of risk can use the algorithm to set cutoffs matched to outcome prevalence, the harms of over- versus under-identifying students, and available intervention resources.
requirements: Districts must decide which outcomes matter, how harmful over- versus under-identification is, and what intervention resources are available before setting algorithm cutoffs.
constraints: The prior performance approach does not provide fine-grained information identifying students at greatest risk.
target_learners: K-12 students at risk of chronic absenteeism, low GPA, course failure, or suspension
target_learning_goals: Accurate early identification of students at academic risk so resources can be targeted before students drop out
examples: The report compares a prior performance early warning system to two algorithm cutoff options: one matching the same percentage of students as the flags, and one identifying the 10 percent of students most at risk.

article_title: Examining the English Language Arts Course Placement System at the College of the Marshall Islands
citation: Shannon, L., Gruber, J., Rentz, B., Vila, C., Erichsen, K., & Nastasi, J. (2026). Examining the English language arts course placement system at the College of the Marshall Islands (REL 2026–006). U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, Regional Educational Laboratory Pacific. https://ies.ed.gov/use-work/resource-library/reports
title: Weight placement measures by their demonstrated predictive value: rely on high school GPA more heavily and drop components that do not predict outcomes
description: This principle holds that course placement systems should weight placement measures in proportion to their demonstrated ability to predict student outcomes, and drop measures that predict nothing. The study found the multiple-choice test and GPA "similarly able to predict passing these credit- bearing courses," while the writing component predicted none, yet the test carried 75 percent of the placement weight. The authors recommend either using GPA alone or dropping the writing component and increasing GPA's weight to streamline placement and cut costs.
requirements: Predictive validity evidence for each placement measure, such as logistic regression against course passing outcomes, as conducted in this study.
constraints: Using GPA alone would come at the cost of slightly reduced placement precision, as the report states.
target_learners: First-year community college students
target_learning_goals: Appropriate placement into credit-bearing versus developmental English language arts coursework
examples: The report recommends CMI consider using only high school GPA to place students or weighting GPA more heavily and removing the writing component to ensure appropriate and logistically efficient course placement.

article_title: Controlling construct-irrelevant factors through computer-based testing: Disengagement, anxiety, & cheating
citation: Steven Wise. (2018). Controlling construct-irrelevant factors through computer-based testing: Disengagement, anxiety, & cheating. Education Inquiry 10(1), 21-33. https://www.tandfonline.com/
title: Weigh benefits against costs, disadvantages, and challenges when deciding whether to move from paper-and-pencil to computer-based tests
description: The article frames the decision to move from paper-and-pencil to computer-based tests as a weighing problem: "A decision of whether to move from paper-and-pencil to computer-based tests is based largely on a careful weighing of the potential benefits of a change against its costs, disadvantages, and challenges." Within that weighing, the article argues that control of construct-irrelevant factors should count among the benefits, since "the potential for expanded control may prove to be one of the most important benefits of computer-based tests."
requirements: Decision-makers must identify and weigh the potential benefits of a change against its costs, disadvantages, and challenges, as the article states.
target_learners: K-12 and other students taking computer-based or paper-and-pencil assessments
target_learning_goals: Valid assessment of achievement through reduced construct-irrelevant variance
examples: The article presents the paper-to-computer transition decision as a trade-off analysis and then examines one benefit side of that analysis: control of disengagement, anxiety, and cheating.

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Weigh the tradeoffs of readily accessible DLP data against the effort of integrating additional data sources
description: The report's fourth consideration addresses data availability: DLPs may lack individual demographic data while collecting school-level covariates such as locale type or Title I status. Researchers should "weigh the tradeoffs and level of effort that may be required to access and integrate additional data," possibly through data sharing agreements, embedded surveys, or LMS/SIS roster linking, and may iterate toward richer data across multiple small-scale studies.
requirements: Understanding whether missing data reflects technical constraints that could be relaxed or is so by design; appropriate permissions and data privacy processes for linking external data
constraints: A DLP may not have access to individual student or teacher demographic data without connecting to other data sources or embedding a survey
target_learners: Education researchers conducting studies in DLPs
target_learning_goals: Obtaining the outcome, demographic, and contextual data needed to answer research questions
examples: Some platforms coordinate data privacy by de-identifying district-provided demographic data so the researcher never sees personally identifiable information

article_title: The Impact of Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) on Student Attendance and Behavior
citation: Gage, N. A., Salomonson, K., Ballew, T., Clavenna-Deane, B., & Grasley-Boy, N. (2024). The Impact of Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) on Student Attendance and Behavior. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: WestEd MTSS coaching model
description: The WestEd MTSS coaching model is a technical-assistance approach in which WestEd subject matter experts "provided coaching for MTSS design and implementation" in partner schools, collecting baseline fidelity-of-implementation data and student-level district data. Unlike models focused only on behavior, the report states it "focuses on coaching schools on both behavior and academic MTSS practices." Coaching began in fall 2022 in three elementary schools in one district and continues through the 2023/24 school year.
requirements: Schools partner with WestEd for on-site coaching and provide student-level demographic, achievement, behavior, and attendance data for evaluation.
constraints: The report is an interim analysis; final data collection and analyses occur in summer 2024, and post-implementation fidelity data were not yet available.
target_learners: Elementary students in a mid-sized Illinois district, including students with learning differences
target_learning_goals: Reducing behavior incidents and absences; strengthening universal, tier 2, and tier 3 academic and behavioral supports
examples: WestEd provided coaching for MTSS design and implementation in three Rock Island elementary schools starting in late spring 2022, with professional development and coaching beginning in fall 2022.

article_title: Building Future-Ready Students: The State of Portraits of a Graduate Frameworks
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). Building future-ready students: The state of Portraits of a Graduate Frameworks. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Policymakers should weigh locally developed versus state-mandated POGs, since local POGs reflect community values while state-mandated POGs offer uniform frameworks and consistent access
description: The brief recommends that policymakers explicitly consider the tradeoff between locally tailored and state-mandated POGs. Locally developed POGs "can reflect community needs and values," while state-mandated POGs "offer a uniform framework that can simplify the support structure for schools and ensure all students have access to a consistent set of competencies and resources." The recommendation follows the brief's finding that both approaches coexist nationally.
requirements: Coordination across multiple agencies and regions for state-led approaches; collaborative community processes for district-led approaches
constraints: The brief frames this as a policy consideration, not a tested comparison of outcomes
target_learners: all high school students
target_learning_goals: developing broad 21st-century competencies defined in POG frameworks
examples: The brief contrasts Indiana's statewide POG mandating academic mastery and career readiness with district-led POGs such as San Marcos Unified's emphasis on adaptability and relational competence

article_title: Student Progress under California State University's Executive Order 1110: A Systemwide Analysis of Outcomes in 2018/19
citation: Bracco, K., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2020). Student progress under California State University's Executive Order 1110: A systemwide analysis of outcomes in 2018/19. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: WestEd course categorization scheme for EO 1110 entry-level WC and QR course types
description: A four-category scheme developed by WestEd researchers to classify how CSU campuses provide additional supports to students in entry-level Written Communication and QR courses under EO 1110. The report states that "the research team found four broad categories of courses": traditional single-semester courses; single-semester courses with additional supports (separate one-unit support modules, embedded support with additional hours, or supplemental instruction); multiterm sequences using two-semester stretch or prerequisite models; and small-unit support courses. Researchers used the scheme to examine student paths toward A2 and B4 requirements and completion rates by placement category.
requirements: Course records must be classifiable into one of the four course types using campus course designations
constraints: The report notes course structures and supports are necessarily broad and cannot capture the nuanced differences from campus to campus
target_learners: CSU entering first-year students placed in Written Communication and Mathematics/Quantitative Reasoning Categories II to IV
target_learning_goals: Completion of entry-level General Education A2 (Written Communication) and B4 (Mathematics/Quantitative Reasoning) requirements in the first year
examples: Researchers used the scheme to compare first-semester course-taking paths (Figures 8-10) and completion rates by course type and placement category (Figures 11-12)

article_title: Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System
citation: The Education Trust–Midwest. (2021). Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System. https://midwest.edtrust.org/advocacy/
title: Weighted student funding formula with transformative equity weights
description: A funding-formula structure in which a base per-pupil amount (in Michigan, the foundation allowance) is multiplied by weights for student need categories, so "every time there is an increase in adequacy funding, there are also automatic increases to equity funding." The report presents a hypothetical example: a $10,000 base with weights of 75% for English Learners, 90% for low-income students, and 160% for students with disabilities yields $17,500, $19,000, and $26,000 per student respectively, and a base increase to $12,000 raises equity dollars automatically. The report argues this resolves the adequacy-versus-equity tension in budget increases.
requirements: Weights must be set at transformative levels based on research and leading-state practice; if weights are too low, every future adequacy investment compounds inequity.
constraints: Michigan's current system is student-based but not a true weighted formula, using varying mechanisms and dollar allotments that require separate legislative action for equity increases.
target_learners: K-12 students, with priority for low-income students, English Learners, students with disabilities, and students in high-poverty or rural communities
target_learning_goals: Automatically closing opportunity gaps as adequacy funding grows, ensuring vulnerable students receive resources needed to achieve at the same high levels as peers
examples: Massachusetts phases in low-income weights up to 105% more ($8,797.76 per pupil in districts with 80% or more low-income students) versus Michigan's $755.78; Maryland phases in 73% for low-income students and 85% for English Learners by fiscal year 2033.
key_sources: The Education Trust–Midwest. (2021). Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System. https://midwest.edtrust.org/advocacy/

article_title: Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System
citation: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://edtrustmidwest.org
title: Fund English Learners through a weighted student funding formula of 80%-100% based on English language proficiency
description: The brief recommends that Michigan lawmakers "implement funding weights ranging from 80% to 100% based on students' language proficiency," in line with leading states and research. target_learning_goals: English language acquisition
access to instructional supports necessary for language acquisition

article_title: Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning
citation: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960
title: Wearable Exam Stress Dataset (PhysioNet) processed into a balanced 328,655-sample multivariate classification dataset
description: The study uses the open-access "A Wearable Exam Stress Dataset for Predicting Cognitive Performance in Real-World Settings" from PhysioNet, collected from 10 college students wearing the Empatica E4 wristband during Midterm 1, Midterm 2, and a Final exam. After preprocessing (pivoting to wide format, removing rows with missing values, grade normalization and categorization into A–F, and undersampling to balance classes at 65,731 observations per grade category), "The final processed dataset contains 328,655 samples" with five physiological predictors (ACC, BVP, EDA, HR, TEMP), three exam-participation indicators, and the grade category as target.
requirements: Grades normalized to a percentage scale and categorized into letter grades A to F; class imbalance handled by undersampling to 65,731 observations per grade category
constraints: Data collected from 10 college students during three exam sessions; rows with missing values were removed
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: predicting academic exam outcomes from physiological stress indicators
examples: Participants wore the E4 wristband during three exam sessions; each midterm lasted 1.5 hours and the final exam 3 hours

article_title: Analysis of Types of Inquiries in Student-AI Interaction: A case study of two CS2 tasks
citation: Matin Amoozadeh and Amin Alipour. (2026). Analysis of Types of Inquiries in Student-AI Interaction: A case study of two CS2 tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17919
title: Web-based CS2 programming environment with integrated GPT-4 AI assistant and interaction logging
description: A web-based programming environment developed for this study in which "The system integrates the programming assign- ment description, a code editor, program execution output, and a conversational AI assistant within one single interface." The AI assistant was powered by GPT-4 accessed through the OpenAI API. The system automatically logged student prompts, AI responses, timestamps, user identifiers, and interaction metadata, enabling analysis of question-asking behavior during two 60-minute lab sessions.
requirements: Students log in, complete a demographic survey, and work on assignments with unlimited AI interaction; assignments must be submitted through the system by the session's time limit.
constraints: The system was used during scheduled laboratory sessions of approximately 60 minutes in a single CS2 course at one university.
target_learners: CS2 (second-year computer science) students, mostly freshmen and sophomores
target_learning_goals: Object-oriented programming in C++, including constructors, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism
examples: Session 1 covered constructors, encapsulation, and method implementation; Session 2 covered inheritance and polymorphism using related Pet and Dog classes.

article_title: What Fidelity Metrics Miss: A Structural Check on Synthetic Educational Data
citation: Inoue, H., & Yasutake, K. (2026). What Fidelity Metrics Miss: A Structural Check on Synthetic Educational Data. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Computers in Education. Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education. https://library.apsce.net
title: Weekly β0 structural check: connected components of a weekly proximity graph over learners tracked across a term
description: A structural summary of how a cohort divides in each week: learners are represented as points in a feature space, connected when Euclidean distance falls below a threshold ε, and β0 counts the connected components of the graph, read as "the number of distinct behavioural groups the cohort forms that week". Tracked across weeks it describes reorganisation rather than level. It requires no optimisation or random seed, is defined for disconnected graphs, and is computed identically on real and synthetic cohorts.
requirements: A choice of threshold ε, which must be controlled because the routine selection rule forces β0/N toward one quarter in every dataset
A complete learner-by-week feature grid with features standardised on a common scale across weeks
constraints: The platform's disclosure rules do not permit component-wise maxima
The authors do not argue β0 is a good measure of learning nor interpret its level educationally
Which structural descriptor serves non-stationarity description best is left open
target_learners: learners in annual cohorts of a lower-secondary study-habit logging system (117 to 120 learners per cohort)
target_learning_goals: describing week-to-week reorganisation of cohort behavioural structure in learning-process data
examples: Applied to four annual cohorts of lower-secondary study-habit logs with weekly study time in six time-of-day bands, and to four OULAD presentations with weekly click counts on six activity types
key_sources: Inoue, H., & Yasutake, K. (2026). What Fidelity Metrics Miss: A Structural Check on Synthetic Educational Data. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Computers in Education. Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27265

article_title: Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology
citation: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105
title: Weighted Bloom's Index and Predicted Exam Score: two new tools for assessing exam equivalence across quarters or courses
description: The study introduces two methods for controlling for exam difficulty in longitudinal course comparisons. The Weighted Bloom's Index "summarizes the average Bloom's level of exam questions weighted by the points possible," computed from independent Bloom's ratings by three trained TAs blind to quarter and hypothesis. The Predicted Exam Score uses three experienced peer-TA graders to predict the average points students would receive on each exam question part. The two metrics were strongly and negatively associated (r = −0.72 for the 18 exams), and both indicated that exams in the highly structured quarters were harder.
requirements: Requires trained raters blind to the study's intent, with norming sessions and decision rules (consensus, majority rule, middle value for sequential ratings, arithmetic average for nonsequential) to assign levels or predicted points to every question part
constraints: Because both indices were computed from data on all exam questions, there is no sample variance and no statistical significance testing is possible when comparing exams
target_learners: STEM education researchers and instructors comparing exams across quarters, courses, or institutions
target_learning_goals: Ensuring that observed changes in student performance reflect course design rather than changes in exam difficulty
examples: Three Bloom's raters each assessed 295 exam questions and assigned 724 Bloom's levels; at least two of three agreed on the identical Bloom's level for 85% of questions rated
key_sources: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105

article_title: Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges
citation: Frederick L. Oswald and Luke Plonsky. (2010). Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges. Annual Review of Applied Linguistics, Volume 30. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0267190510000115
title: Plan meta-analyses carefully, use sound statistical methods, and ground them in relevant theory so they can inform theory, research, practice, and policy
description: This principle holds that a meta-analysis in applied linguistics delivers critical information only under three conditions: it must be "well planned," "employs sound statistical methods," and be "based on a thorough understanding of relevant theory." When these hold, the review states the meta-analysis "can provide critical information that informs theory as well as future research, practice, and policy." The article presents this as the general condition for meta-analysis to benefit SLA.
requirements: Careful planning of the meta-analysis
Sound statistical methods
Thorough understanding of relevant theory
constraints: The informative value is conditional; the article does not claim all meta-analyses provide critical information
target_learners: applied linguistics and SLA researchers
research consumers in language education
target_learning_goals: producing and interpreting trustworthy quantitative research syntheses in language learning research
examples: The review's concluding general statement ties well-planned, statistically sound, theory-based meta-analysis to informing theory, research, practice, and policy

article_title: Comparing frameworks for 21st century skills
citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Dede's category system for Web 2.0 tools
description: Dede (2009b) delineated a category system for current Web 2.0 tools with three categories: Sharing (communal bookmarking, photo/video sharing, social networking, writers' workshops/fanfiction), Thinking (blogs, podcasts, online discussion forums), and Co-Creating (wikis/collaborative file creation, mashups/collective media creation, collaborative social change communities). The chapter describes "a loose progression from top to bottom", with sharing leading to thinking together and then collective action by sophisticated groups seeking change.
requirements: Tools support communities of contributors rather than one-way presentation of material
target_learners: Internet-using learners and communities of contributors
target_learning_goals: Collaboration, knowledge co-creation, and collective action
examples: The nine media listed span sharing tools like social networking through co-creating tools like collaborative social change communities

article_title: Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment
citation: Mayer, I. (2018). Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment. Simulation & Gaming, 49(6), 602-619. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878118770831
title: In game-based team assessment, weight avoidable mistakes over team speed
description: Because in-game time and distance are largely driven by team structure such as age and game experience, while avoidable mistakes reflect team cohesiveness and task quality, assessors should focus feedback and judgement on errors rather than speed. The author states: "we should put less emphasis on how fast a team is, and more on how many avoidable mistakes a team makes, for example how many times a known mistake is repeated." Partial validation of the game gives guidance to trainers and assessors on which indicators to trust.
requirements: A game that logs avoidable mistakes unobtrusively, where repeating a known ineffective action is detectable
constraints: Validated for TEAMUP only; results have not been compared with other digital team games and cannot be generalised
target_learners: professional teams in training and assessment programmes
trainers and assessors using serious games
target_learning_goals: valid team assessment and debriefing feedback
examples: In TEAMUP sessions, individual and team scores for time, distance and avoidable mistakes were shown on a central screen to trigger and deepen the plenary debriefing discussion

citation: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123

description: The article proposes that implicit metacognition enables adoption of a we-mode, in which a person's saliency/value map is automatically modified so object values approximate the average of the group derived from implicit estimates of others' goals, knowledge and beliefs. Implicit estimates of other group members' goals, knowledge and beliefs

description: Stahl notes the 1980s conception of transactivity by Wegner and others was a psychological theory in which individuals hold different knowledge and transact to assist recall of stored information through meta-knowledge about what each other knows. Learning outcomes classified by kind of knowledge and level of understanding

promotion of peace

article_title: A criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with alternative suggestions.
citation: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale
title: Weight test scores according to each test's significance as a measure of intelligence before combining them
description: Because tests differ in fineness of gradation, time devoted, and dependence on non-intellectual factors, the article holds that "the tests should be weighted, therefore, according to their significance as measures of intelligence." Two weighting methods are described: partial correlation against an external criterion such as teachers' intelligence estimates, and, viewed as perhaps better, deriving weights from the amounts of intercorrelation among the tests taken singly, which approximates how strongly each test measures the factor common to all. Weighted absolute grades are then summed into a point-score.
requirements: Weights may be derived either from an external criterion via regression methods or from the tests' intercorrelations; weights must keep the same proportions whatever their sum
constraints: Equating test scores on the absolute scale is unsafe until test elements are graduated so difficulty increments between elements are very nearly equal
target_learners: children and adults taking intelligence test batteries
target_learning_goals: accurate composite measurement of general intelligence
examples: The article's Table V illustrates a weighted average of 84 versus an unweighted 80 for a seven-test series with weights from 1 to 5, and Table VI converts sentence-test performance into weighted points

title: Web-based crowdsourced version of the sequential finger tapping task on Amazon Mechanical Turk
description: A web-based implementation of the well-characterized sequential finger tapping task (5-item keypress sequence, 4-1-3-2-4, with the nondominant left hand) programmed in Psytoolkit, administered on Amazon Mechanical Turk with participants using their own computers. It proved "useful to study human motor learning dynamics at a large scale", enabling samples of hundreds of participants (e.g., N = 389) with data collection averaging 16 h and 26 min per experiment, and replicated the in-lab learning-curve shape and microdynamics.

constraints: A proportion of participants did not follow instructions and had to be excluded; variability is higher than in-lab at comparable sample sizes; designs requiring prolonged task durations or longitudinal measurements need extra care; groups must be properly randomized given rapid changes in worker pool composition

target_learning_goals: measurement of microscale motor skill learning dynamics in early acquisition

title: Wearable dual-channel EEG headband setup for real-classroom brain recording
description: A portable EEG data-collection setup in which students wore "a dual-channel headband with dry electrodes... to record EEG at Fp1 and Fp2 over the forehead at a sampling rate of 250 Hz" during regular Math and Chinese lessons. Headbands were fitted before and removed after each 40-minute session, enabling EEG acquisition from an entire class across a full semester (39 sessions over 4 months). citation: Blanchard, E. G. (2015). Socio-Cultural Imbalances in AIED Research: Investigations, Implications and Opportunities. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0027-7
title: WEIRD subjects as outliers: the generalization-risk account of imbalanced psychology samples
description: The article adopts Henrich et al.'s (2010a) account that WEIRD populations are not representative of humankind: members of industrialized societies "frequently score as outliers" on basic psychological functions, and WEIRD subjects "may often be the worst population from which to make generalizations". The account distinguishes four levels of comparison (industrialized vs small-scale, WEIRD vs non-WEIRD, Americans vs other WEIRD, American students vs other Americans) and holds that universal learning processes exist but their outputs depend on socio-cultural features. The article uses it to argue that AIED findings generalized from WEIRD samples carry untested assumptions.
requirements: comparative studies across populations, since the account calls for consideration of human diversity to become more systematic
constraints: exclusive reliance on WEIRD samples may be adequate when seeking existential proofs that a process exists

target_learning_goals: valid generalization of learning-research findings across cultures

article_title: A Comparison of Internet-Based Learning and Traditional Classroom Lecture to Learn CPR for Continuing Medical Education
citation: Hemmati, N., Omrani, S., & Hemmati, N. (2013). A comparison of internet-based learning and traditional classroom lecture to learn CPR for continuing medical education. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 14(1). https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: Design Internet-based CME content well, with interactivity and multimedia, so it can serve as an effective component or supplement to CME

title: WebQuest: an inquiry-oriented, Internet-based lesson format with six essential parts
description: A WebQuest is an inquiry-oriented lesson format in which most or all learner information comes from the web, developed by Bernie Dodge in 1995. It comprises six essential parts: "introduction, task, process, resources, evaluation, and conclusion", with the introduction posing the Big Question and the evaluation section describing how performance is assessed. In this study the experimental group used WebQuest activities during science lessons on ecosystems and the solar system.

description: The article frames the WebQuest's critical steps as "a frame for a scaffolded learning environment" whose purpose is to establish a setting where students gain higher order thinking skills using Internet resources with help from guided process steps. It connects this to the constructivist approach, in which students construct their own knowledge through technology during learning, and notes the structure overcomes drawbacks of open Internet use such as eliminating useless information and recognizing quality information.
requirements: Guided process steps and teacher guidance so students can gain higher order thinking skills from Internet resources
constraints: Some WebQuests add a teacher page; Young and Wilson added "what do you think" and "Share and compare" parts, showing the structure is adaptable

description: The article presents WebQuest, introduced by Bernie Dodge in 1995, as "a new teaching strategy of the constructivist approach that uses computer environment", designed to ensure meaningful learning by combining technology with constructivism. citation: Rohollahzadeh Ebadi, M., Mohd Saad, M. R., & Abedalaziz, N. (2013). Explicit Form Focus Instruction: The Effects on Implicit and Explicit Knowledge of ESL Learners. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(4). https://www.moj-es.net
title: Weak interface position: corrective feedback facilitating explicit learning also facilitates implicit learning
description: The weak interface position (attributed to Ellis, 2006) holds that explicit and implicit knowledge are partially connected, so attention and consciousness raised by corrective feedback benefit both types of learning. The article states that "corrective feedback, by providing a kind of attention and consciousness in learners, not only facilitates explicit learning and explicit memory, but also implicit learning and implicit memory". The study's finding that metalinguistic feedback improved both implicit and explicit knowledge is offered as support for this position, alongside Schmidt's noticing hypothesis, under which noticing the gap between interlanguage and target forms facilitates grammatical restructuring.
requirements: Corrective feedback must draw learners' attention to gaps between their interlanguage forms and target forms for the facilitative effect to occur
constraints: The article's support comes from one classroom experiment on five partially acquired structures with adult learners over 20 years old
target_learners: adult lower-intermediate ESL learners
target_learning_goals: implicit and explicit knowledge of English grammatical structures
examples: The study measured implicit and explicit knowledge separately with EOIT, TGJT, UGJT and MKT and found significant posttest gains on both types after metalinguistic feedback.

title: Weak central coherence as a cognitive-style account of reading comprehension difficulties in high-functioning ASD
description: The article draws on central coherence theory (Frith, 1989; Frith & Happé, 1994), which holds that students with ASD do not spontaneously perceive complex stimuli as coherent, meaningful wholes, showing an exaggerated focus on details. The theory explains difficulties perceiving the general meaning of texts, underdeveloped general vocabulary, and trouble interpreting context-dependent words such as pronouns. main idea identification
examples: The pilot intervention taught main idea identification and text structure to compensate for students' undue focus on details

description: The article recommends that educators designing written assessments balance the diversity benefits of including ethnicity against its measured costs. citation: Drovandi Aaron, Sheader Elizabeth, Kingston Margaret. (2026). Integrated Team-Based Learning in a UK Undergraduate Medical Programme. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70470
title: Weekly TBL cycle structure: opening session, mid-week teaching activities, and closing session with IRAT/TRAT, application exercises and expert panel.
description: TBL is delivered in weekly cycles, commencing with a 1-h 'opening' session involving the whole cohort attending a single interactive lecture theatre event, with two to three academics presenting core information through simulation, narrated roleplay or interactive exercises. Mid-week teaching activities are then provided, followed by a 2-h 'closing' session involving students working in teams of six, in a larger learning community of 8–10 teams per room. constraints: Students valued discussions for the IRAT/TRAT and AES and felt more time was needed to delve into questions and answers more comprehensively.

target_learning_goals: Gauging breadth and depth of knowledge, applying knowledge to clinical scenarios, and engaging with expert clinical perspectives on weekly themes
examples: The expert panel, composed of basic science and clinical specialists, answer 'burning questions' raised which could be submitted by students using LAMS as well as concepts the cohort struggled with.

article_title: Why academic selection fails to protect against physician burnout: a brief research report from a 25-year longitudinal programme.
citation: Walkiewicz M. (2026). Why academic selection fails to protect against physician burnout: a brief research report from a 25-year longitudinal programme. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1836438
title: Treat wellbeing as a support problem rather than a selection problem in medical education
description: The article recommends that medical education shift investment from selection toward systematic support and resilience-building, because "Academic selection ensures competence but does not prevent burnout." It proposes four reform directions: confidential early self-assessment of psychological resources, universal curriculum-integrated coping-skills training framed as professional development, systematic longitudinal wellbeing monitoring, and structural reform of practices that function as psychosocial hazards.
requirements: Interventions must be framed as professional development rather than remedial therapy, and self-assessment designed to build metacognitive awareness rather than to gatekeep.
constraints: The principal findings originate from a single national and institutional context, which limits generalisability; replication outside Central Europe is needed.
target_learners: medical students
medical schools and workforce-policy makers
target_learning_goals: maintaining student wellbeing and occupational sustainability throughout medical education
examples: The article recommends transition from numerical grading to pass/fail assessment in pre-clinical years, which has been shown to reduce stress without compromising academic performance, and reform of the hidden curriculum that teaches emotional suppression as a marker of professionalism.

article_title: Comparing the Weighted Gain Score and a Rasch-Based Approach for Estimating Learning Outcomes in Medical Education: Quantitative Study.
citation: Rauf A, Backhaus J, Hammer S, König S. (2026). Comparing the Weighted Gain Score and a Rasch-Based Approach for Estimating Learning Outcomes in Medical Education: Quantitative Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/75516
title: The Weighted Gain Score metric: a computationally simple learning gain estimator with µ as an adjustment coefficient
description: The Weighted Gain Score is a learning gain metric for pretest-posttest designs that applies a weighting coefficient 'pre/µ' to linearly transform the difference between pretest and posttest percentage scores, thereby adjusting for pretest variability. Formally, WGS=(post−pre)×(pre/μ). The article reinterprets µ not solely as the cohort's average pretest score but as an adjustment coefficient that functions as a scaling parameter, where higher values of µ lead to smaller gain estimates and lower values produce larger estimates. The WGS requires substantially lower computational complexity than Rasch-based approaches and can be applied to both small and large datasets.
requirements: Requires pretest and posttest percentage scores; µ constrained to integer values between 1 and 100
constraints: A student with a pretest score of zero receives a calculated learning gain of zero regardless of posttest performance
target_learners: Medical students in pretest-posttest educational evaluations
target_learning_goals: Estimating learning gain in pretest-posttest educational designs

citation: Karakoç Hediye, Ozkan Hava. (2026). The effect of wearable simulated birth model on students’ empathy and privacy protection levels: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education, 26, 383. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08441-8
title: Wearable simulated birth model with structured seven-week counseling intervention for midwifery students
description: A two-component educational intervention combining a wearable simulated maternity model with a seven-week structured counseling program. title: WeChat-PBL: an online problem-based learning mode for hematology postgraduates built on the WeChat app with micro clinical cases
description: WeChat-PBL is a pedagogical mode in which "Micro clinical cases including clinical characteristics and relevant questions were uploaded to the WeChat-PBL group 3 days before class." Students in groups of 6 or 7 plus a tutor prepare PowerPoints, present them via WeChat video conferencing, and discuss by sending text, images, voice recordings, videos, or documents, while the tutor summarizes and explains. The mode was implemented with 48 hematology postgraduates and 7 tutors at Zhongnan Hospital, Wuhan University, from August to October 2020, and evaluated for feasibility and acceptability.
requirements: Students need their own mobile phones with the WeChat app installed and familiarity with WeChat in the PBL context
Clinical doctors with 1 or more years of experience in traditional PBL teaching serve as tutors
constraints: Evaluated only with postgraduates majoring in hematology at a single institution
The article notes the limited sample size and calls for further comprehensive, large-scale, and high-quality studies

teamwork and communication
self-directed learning and scientific research abilities

title: Weighted error protocol ranking errors by severity (1–3) and categorizing them as handling, knowledge, or both
description: An evaluation instrument derived by the authors for comparing training instructions: "an error protocol that contains a list of possible errors and ranks each of them with a factor between 1 and 3 based according to their severity". Errors are further categorized as handling errors (related to individual dexterity), knowledge errors (caused by lack of attention to task-related information), or both. The article reports that deriving this protocol provided valuable insights on the effectiveness of training instructions.
requirements: A list of possible errors with severity factors between 1 and 3, and categorization of each error as handling, knowledge, or both
constraints: Differences between instruction types occurred only for 1-point and 2-point errors; both instruction types resulted in two 3-point errors
